todays_goal: Advance where mastery is secure, make every subject more visual, keep French as the daily review subject, teach area before testing it, and launch a clear, fun, laptop-only ScoutLab builder project.

lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.lesson_title: Area: Square Units, Rectangles, and Right Triangles
lessons.previous_learning: September 29 work showed strong understanding of units, horizontal/vertical coordinate distance, and perimeter. Area had intentionally been held until prerequisite teaching was complete.
lessons.course_context: Introduce area visually as coverage by unit squares before using formulas.
learning_objectives: Explain square units
Find rectangle area
Find right-triangle area as half a rectangle
Use coordinate distance to find side lengths before area
Distinguish linear units from square units
lessons.why_it_matters: Area connects coordinate distance to geometry while making measurement units meaningful.

vocabulary.definition: a 1-by-1 square used to measure area
the amount of flat space inside a shape
a chosen side of a triangle
the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex

lessons.written_instruction: Teach the picture first: area counts 1-by-1 squares inside a shape. Rectangle area is rows times squares per row. A right triangle is half of a matching rectangle.

worked_examples.title: Count squares
worked_examples.explanation: Three rows of four unit squares.

guided_practice.prompt: Draw and solve a 5 by 4 rectangle.
Find area of a 9 by 3 rectangle.
Find area of a right triangle with base 8 and height 6.

independent_practice.prompt: Find the area of a 12 by 5 rectangle.
Find the area of a right triangle with base 10 and height 4.
Find width, height, and area of the coordinate rectangle in the packet.
Explain how yesterday's distance skill helps you find coordinate-grid area.

exit_ticket.prompt: What does one square unit mean?
Find the area of an 8 by 7 rectangle.
Find the area of a right triangle with base 12 and height 5.
Why is 24 units different from 24 square units?
exit_ticket.answer: Units measure length; square units measure area.

lessons.voice_prompt: VISUAL FIRST. Draw unit squares before using formulas. Use a different rectangle and triangle from the assigned work. Ask Atticus to explain why square units are used. Teach rectangle area before triangle area. Never ask for an untaught area type. Keep assigned answers protected.
lessons.teacher_notes: Advance after strong September 29 distance/perimeter performance.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.previous_learning: September 29 writing was strong overall. Continue precision by requiring every important evidence sentence to be followed by what it shows.
lessons.course_context: Move from isolated claim/evidence/reasoning into a visually organized evidence ladder.
learning_objectives: Write a claim
Select exact evidence
Explain what evidence shows
Use cautious language such as supports or strengthens
Write a conclusion that matches the evidence
lessons.why_it_matters: Evidence is only useful in analytical writing when the writer explains its meaning.

vocabulary.definition: gives evidence in favor of an explanation

lessons.written_instruction: Use the ladder: CLAIM -> EVIDENCE -> WHAT IT SHOWS -> EVIDENCE -> WHAT IT SHOWS -> CONCLUSION.

worked_examples.title: Motor evidence
worked_examples.explanation: The test directly checks the first explanation.

worked_examples.title: Battery evidence
worked_examples.explanation: Changing the battery changes the outcome.

guided_practice.prompt: Write a claim and two exact test results from The Two Batteries.

independent_practice.prompt: Write an 8-9 sentence paragraph from the ladder and revise one sentence after reading aloud.

exit_ticket.prompt: Which sentence in your paragraph does the most reasoning, and why?
exit_ticket.answer: Answer varies; must identify a sentence that interprets evidence.

lessons.voice_prompt: Use the whiteboard to display the ladder. For each evidence statement ask only: What does that show? Do not let two evidence sentences appear in a row without reasoning. Encourage supports/strengthens/weakens instead of proves unless certainty is justified. Do not dictate the assigned paragraph.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.previous_learning: September 29 showed much better control but a remaining subject mismatch: a tu prompt was answered with a vous construction. Oral mastery was not visible in submitted work.
lessons.course_context: Today's review subject. Consolidate subject -> aller -> infinitive, then negatives and Est-ce que questions.
learning_objectives: Match pronouns to aller forms
Keep action verbs infinitive
Form a negative futur proche sentence
Form an Est-ce que futur proche question
lessons.why_it_matters: Automatic control of the pattern allows attention to shift from grammar to meaning.
lessons.written_instruction: Use the visual build: SUBJECT -> ALLER -> INFINITIVE -> MEANING.

worked_examples.title: Negative
worked_examples.problem: We are not going to play.
worked_examples.explanation: Negation wraps around the conjugated aller form.

independent_practice.prompt: Translate six futur proche prompts from the packet, including one negative and one Est-ce que question.

exit_ticket.prompt: Say six new futur proche sentences without looking.

lessons.voice_prompt: VISUAL + ORAL FIRST. Show SUBJECT -> ALLER -> INFINITIVE on the whiteboard. For each cue ask for the subject first, then the aller form, then the infinitive. If the subject is wrong, stop there and repair it before continuing. Do not give the full assigned sentence.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.previous_learning: September 29 work showed strong understanding of angle in = angle out, the normal, and the relationship between two reflections.
lessons.course_context: Apply reflection visually in a two-mirror engineering design.
learning_objectives: Apply reflection at two mirrors
Draw a new normal at each hit point
Predict how rotating a mirror changes the path
Explain a designed light path
lessons.why_it_matters: The same reflection law can be used to design practical optical systems.

vocabulary.definition: the route a ray follows through the system
the point where the ray hits a mirror

lessons.written_instruction: Design SOURCE -> Mirror 1 -> Mirror 2 -> TARGET. Draw and label both normals and check angle in = angle out at both mirrors.

worked_examples.title: Two-mirror path
worked_examples.problem: Reach a target around a corner.
worked_examples.solution: Use mirror 1 to redirect toward mirror 2, then mirror 2 toward target.
worked_examples.explanation: The outgoing ray from mirror 1 becomes the incoming ray at mirror 2.

independent_practice.prompt: Explain how rotating mirror 1 changes the rest of the path.

exit_ticket.prompt: What does the outgoing ray from Mirror 1 become at Mirror 2?
Why does rotating a mirror change the reflected direction?
exit_ticket.answer: It changes the normal and therefore the reflected path.

lessons.voice_prompt: VISUAL ENGINEERING MODE. Draw source and target first, then one mirror at a time. Ask Atticus to predict the ray before drawing it. At mirror 2, explicitly ask for a new normal. Do not draw the assigned finished maze for him.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.previous_learning: September 29 Builder work was not submitted and prior QA-style instructions were too abstract for a 12-year-old.
lessons.course_context: Start a fresh, visible, fun vibe-coding project with explicit child-friendly steps.
learning_objectives: Describe a product goal in natural language
Create a three-card comparison interface with a coding AI
Edit simple player data
Test compare and shortlist behavior
Explain one design choice
lessons.why_it_matters: Atticus practices directing AI to build useful software, testing visible behavior, and improving a product without needing to know syntax first.

vocabulary.definition: the first working version with only the core features
a saved set of players you want to consider further

lessons.written_instruction: Laptop only. Mission: build ScoutLab, a three-player football comparison tool. Atticus is the product designer; the coding AI writes the code.

worked_examples.title: Child-friendly build request
worked_examples.problem: How do I tell the coding AI what to make?
worked_examples.solution: Describe the page, the visible controls, what happens when Compare is pressed, and what Shortlist should remember.
worked_examples.explanation: Good vibe coding is clear product direction, not writing syntax.

guided_practice.prompt: Choose three players and one visual style.

independent_practice.prompt: Create a new ScoutLab browser project using the copy-ready prompt in the packet.
Change one rating, press Compare, and verify the category leader updates.
Shortlist one player and verify the choice remains visible.
If something breaks, tell Virgil what you clicked, what you expected, and what happened; let Virgil translate that into a fix request.

exit_ticket.prompt: Demo three players, change one rating, compare, shortlist one player, and explain why that player fits your team.

lessons.voice_prompt: KID-FRIENDLY BUILDER MODE. Do not use QA jargon unless Atticus asks. Start by saying the mission in one sentence. Then give exactly one action at a time: open new project, paste prompt, choose players, test Compare, test Shortlist. If something breaks, ask Atticus only: what did you click, what did you expect, what happened? YOU translate his answer into a precise fix request for the coding AI. Keep the whiteboard as a simple checklist. Do not take over the build.
lessons.teacher_notes: New project deliberately replaces abstract QA-only work with creative product building.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.previous_learning: September 29 work showed strong understanding of Alexandria, cultural exchange, and major Hellenistic thinkers.
lessons.course_context: Transition from the Hellenistic world into Ancient Rome through geography.
learning_objectives: Locate Rome on the Italian Peninsula
Explain advantages of the Tiber River
Explain the value of farmland and hills
Explain central Mediterranean location
Avoid claiming geography alone caused Roman success
lessons.why_it_matters: Geography shaped opportunities and constraints for early Rome.

vocabulary.definition: the peninsula extending into the Mediterranean where Rome developed
the river beside which Rome developed

lessons.written_instruction: Rome developed near the Tiber River on the Italian Peninsula. Farmland, hills, river access, and a central Mediterranean location offered useful advantages, but geography did not guarantee success.

worked_examples.title: Cause and effect
worked_examples.problem: How can a river help a city?
worked_examples.explanation: A geographic feature matters because of what people can do with it.

independent_practice.prompt: Explain how the Tiber could help Rome.
Explain why hills could help early Rome.
Explain why geography alone is not a complete explanation of Roman success.

exit_ticket.prompt: In 4 sentences, explain two geographic advantages Rome had and why each mattered.
exit_ticket.answer: Answers should connect two accurate features to specific advantages.

lessons.voice_prompt: VISUAL FIRST. Use the whiteboard as a simple hub: ROME in the middle with arrows to Tiber, farmland, hills, and Mediterranean access. For each feature ask: what advantage could this give? Do not let geography become a one-cause explanation.
lessons.teacher_notes: New Ancient Rome unit begins today.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.previous_learning: September 29 work showed good Chapters 3-4 comprehension with some need for tighter evidence precision.
lessons.course_context: Continue from the current page without spoilers and use a visual clue network after reading.
learning_objectives: Read independently for 25 minutes
Record one exact clue or event
Explain what the clue suggests
Update a theory based on evidence
Form one new question
lessons.why_it_matters: Mystery reading improves when theories change in response to specific evidence.

vocabulary.definition: a current explanation that may change as new evidence appears

lessons.written_instruction: Read first. Afterward, connect CHARACTER -> CLUE -> WHAT IT MEANS -> QUESTION -> THEORY.

independent_practice.prompt: Read The Westing Game for 25 minutes from the current page.
Complete one visual clue board using a specific event from today's reading.

exit_ticket.prompt: Did today's clue strengthen, weaken, or change your theory? Explain in one sentence.

lessons.voice_prompt: Stay quiet during reading unless Atticus asks for a brief word definition. After reading, use the visual clue network and ask one question at a time. Require one exact clue and no spoilers beyond what he read today.
lessons.teacher_notes: Continue reading from current location; do not force a chapter number.
